docs.text: ROS 2 Tutorial ¶ Pranav Bhounsule · tiny.cc/pranavb · Welcome! This site walks through ROS 2 (Jazzy) hands-on, using three small robot examples instead of toy "hello world" nodes: ddrive — a differential-drive robot, used to teach core ROS 2 concepts (nodes, topics, publishers/subscribers, services, actions, parameters, launch files). twolink — a two-link planar arm, used to teach RViz and forward / inverse kinematics. dbpendulum — a double pendulum, used to teach Gazebo Sim physics and, later, torque control via ros2_control . How the site is organized ¶ Installation — environment setup (ROS 2, workspace, dependencies). ROS2 Basics with ddrive — core concepts (nodes, topics, messages, publishers/subscribers, services, actions, parameters, packages, and launch files), then ddrive , ddrive_ik , and ddrive_ik_msgs (services & actions), finishing with an exercise (mecanum car). RViz Basics with twolink — twolink (joint-space sliders) and twolink_ik (Cartesian target tracking), finishing with an exercise (three-link IK with orientation). Gazebo Basics with dbpendulum — dbpendulum (passive, chaotic double pendulum) and dbpendulum_ctrl (feedback-linearization torque control), finishing with an exercise (single-pendulum swing-up). Use the navigation on the left to jump to any section. Package downloads Each package page includes a download link to that package's zipped source, hosted alongside this site.

docs.text: Installation ¶ This site uses Docker on every host OS — Ubuntu, macOS, and Windows — instead of installing ROS 2 directly on your machine. The reason is version control: your host OS might not match a given ROS 2 release (Ubuntu 20.04 can't run Jazzy natively, for example), but a Docker image gives you exactly the ROS 2 distro you want, independent of what your host is running. Every command on this site sources ROS 2 via $ROS_DISTRO instead of a hardcoded name like foxy or jazzy , so the exact same commands work no matter which distro's image you're running. You'll set this once inside the container, in 1.3 : source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash and, once you've built at least one package: source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash 1.1 Install Docker ¶ Pick your host OS below. All three converge on the same checkpoint: a working docker command. Ubuntu (or any Linux host) ¶ Docker Engine installs directly — no VM layer needed: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg echo \ "deb [arch= $( dpkg --print-architecture ) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] \ https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $( . /etc/os-release && echo " $VERSION_CODENAME " ) stable" \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null sudo apt update sudo apt install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io sudo usermod -aG docker $USER Log out and back in (or reboot) so your user picks up the docker group, then confirm: docker run hello-world macOS ¶ Install Docker Desktop for Mac — download the .dmg , drag it into Applications, and launch it once to finish setup. Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) If you're on an Apple Silicon Mac, you'll confirm you're pulling a native arm64 image later, in 1.2 — an emulated (x86_64) image runs noticeably slower. This check does not apply to Intel Macs, which only ever pull native x86_64 images. Confirm Docker is working: docker run hello-world Windows ¶ Docker Desktop on Windows needs WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux) as its backend — which conveniently also gives you a real Ubuntu shell, so every bash command on this site works unmodified. Open PowerShell as Administrator and run: wsl - -install Reboot when prompted. This installs WSL2 and a default Ubuntu distro. Install Docker Desktop for Windows . During setup, make sure "Use WSL 2 based engine" is checked (this is the default on modern installs). In Docker Desktop, go to Settings → Resources → WSL Integration and enable integration with your Ubuntu distro. Restart Docker Desktop. Open the Ubuntu app from the Start Menu — this is your WSL2 terminal. Run every command on this site from the Ubuntu (WSL2) terminal Not PowerShell, not Command Prompt. From here on, ~/ros2_ws means your WSL2 Ubuntu home directory, and every command on this site behaves exactly as written for Mac/Linux. From the Ubuntu terminal, confirm Docker is reachable: docker run hello-world 1.2 Pull the image and create the container ¶ docker pull tiryoh/ros2-desktop-vnc:jazzy Swap jazzy for whichever ROS 2 distro you want — check available tags at hub.docker.com/r/tiryoh/ros2-desktop-vnc/tags . Whatever you pick here is also what you'll set $ROS_DISTRO to in 1.3 — keep the two in sync. Apple Silicon: confirm it's native arm64 docker image inspect tiryoh/ros2-desktop-vnc:jazzy | grep Architecture should print "Architecture": "arm64" . Create a folder that will become your ROS 2 workspace, then start the container: mkdir -p ~/ros2_ws/src docker run -d --name ros2_jazzy \ --shm-size = 512m \ -p 6080 :80 \ -v ~/ros2_ws:/home/ubuntu/ros2_ws \ -e VNC_PASSWORD = ubuntu \ tiryoh/ros2-desktop-vnc:jazzy Naming the container ros2_jazzy (rather than after any one package) keeps it obvious which ROS 2 distro it's running — rename it to match if you pull a different distro's image, e.g. ros2_humble . Log into the Ubuntu desktop ¶ Open http://localhost:6080 in a browser. You'll land on a VNC password prompt — enter ubuntu (the password set above). You should land on a full Ubuntu desktop with a terminal on the taskbar. Everything else on this site — every ros2 run , every colcon build — happens in terminals opened from that desktop, not in your host OS's own terminal. Where ~/ros2_ws actually lives ¶ The -v ~/ros2_ws:/home/ubuntu/ros2_ws flag maps one real folder on your host to a path inside the container: On your host Inside the container ~/ros2_ws (Mac/Linux), or your WSL2 Ubuntu ~/ros2_ws (Windows) /home/ubuntu/ros2_ws The container's user is ubuntu , whose home directory is /home/ubuntu — so /home/ubuntu/ros2_ws is also just ~/ros2_ws from a terminal inside the container. In other words, ~/ros2_ws means the exact same folder whether you type it on your host or in a VNC desktop terminal — they're not two copies, they're one folder viewed from two places. Anything you colcon build inside the container ( build/ , install/ , log/ ) is written straight onto your host's disk, and any file you drop into ~/ros2_ws on your host shows up instantly inside the container. This is also why your workspace survives even if you delete the container entirely — the folder was never inside the container to begin with. Everyday startup (after the first time) ¶ You only need to docker run once. After that: docker start ros2_jazzy then back to http://localhost:6080 . Whatever you installed inside the container earlier — including the optional matplotlib/numpy setup below — is still there, since docker start reuses the same container rather than creating a new one. To stop it when you're done for the day: docker stop ros2_jazzy If you ever need to start completely fresh (wipes anything installed inside the container, but never touches ~/ros2_ws on your host): docker rm -f ros2_jazzy # then re-run the docker run command above 1.3 Set $ROS_DISTRO and verify ROS 2 works ¶ Inside the container's desktop terminal: echo 'export ROS_DISTRO=jazzy' >> ~/.bashrc # match whatever distro you pulled in 1.2 source ~/.bashrc echo $ROS_DISTRO That last line should print your distro name back. From now on, every terminal on this site starts the same way: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash Verify: talker / listener ¶ The real test that ROS 2 is alive isn't that the commands exist — it's that two independent nodes can actually publish and subscribe to each other. Open two terminals inside the container's desktop. Terminal 1: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker Terminal 2: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener Terminal 1 should print Publishing: 'Hello World: N' once a second, and Terminal 2 should print I heard: [Hello World: N] right behind it. Ctrl+C both once you've seen it work. Once you've built at least one workspace package (starting on the next page), every terminal also needs: source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash matplotlib/numpy (only if a node needs them) ¶ Not every package on this site needs these — install them inside the container only when a node actually imports them (e.g. ddrive 's visualizer node): pip3 install matplotlib numpy --break-system-packages NumPy/matplotlib version mismatch On newer Ubuntu/ROS combinations, a pip-installed NumPy 2.x can conflict with an apt-installed matplotlib built against NumPy 1.x, causing an ImportError when a node imports matplotlib. If you hit this, either pin NumPy down: pip3 install "numpy<2" --break-system-packages --force-reinstall or use apt for both instead of pip: sudo apt install -y python3-matplotlib python3-numpy

docs.text: 2.1 Fundamentals ¶ From Python functions to ROS 2 ¶ If you already know Python, one useful way to understand ROS 2 is to start with something familiar: functions . A normal Python program might look like this: def main (): x = read_sensor () u = controller ( x ) send_command ( u ) The programmer controls the sequence. main() calls one function, which calls another, and the program proceeds step by step. A robot is different. A robot operates in the real world, where time keeps moving. Sensors continuously produce data, controllers continuously compute commands, and other parts of the system need to keep running. ROS 2 provides a way to organize this continuous computation. A ROS 2 node can be thought of as an active computational program that stays alive and responds to events. This is not a literal definition of a node, but it is a useful mental model when coming from traditional Python programming. 1. Nodes: active computational blocks ¶ A node is a running ROS 2 program that performs a particular responsibility. For a differential-drive robot, you might have: a localization node that estimates the robot's position, a planner node that determines a path, a controller node that computes velocity commands, a simulator node that moves the robot, a visualization node that displays the robot's state. Each node can operate independently. This is different from a traditional program in which functions are called directly: Traditional Python main() | +--> localization() | +--> planner() | +--> controller() In ROS 2, the components are independent: ROS 2 Localization node ---> topic ---> Controller node | | topic v Simulator node The nodes do not need to directly call one another. They communicate through ROS 2's communication mechanisms. A node is more than one function ¶ The analogy to a function is useful, but a node is not literally a function. A Python ROS 2 node is commonly implemented as a class containing several functions, such as: subscriber callback functions, timer callback functions, service callback functions, action callbacks. The node stays alive, while ROS 2 calls the appropriate function when something happens. For example, a controller might have a callback that executes whenever a new robot pose arrives: new pose arrives | v controller callback() | +--> compute control | +--> publish cmd_vel So a useful mental model is: A node is an active computational block containing functions that respond to events. 2. Topics: communication channels ¶ A topic is a named communication channel. Topics do not perform the computation themselves. They carry messages between nodes. Think of the analogy with a traditional function: Python function input --> function --> output In ROS 2: Node A --> topic --> Node B The topic is like the connection between the two computational blocks. For example, a localization node might publish the robot's estimated position on the odom topic: Localization node | | publishes pose v /odom | | subscribed by v Controller node The controller does not directly call the localization node. It simply subscribes to /odom . This separation is important because the publisher does not need to know who is listening. Topics are asynchronous ¶ ROS 2 communication is generally asynchronous. A publisher sends a message when it has one. A subscriber receives it and ROS 2 schedules the appropriate callback. The two nodes do not have to execute at exactly the same time. This is different from a normal Python function call, where the caller waits for the function to execute and return. 3. Messages: the data being exchanged ¶ A message defines the type and structure of data being sent on a topic. For example, a topic might carry: a position, a velocity, a laser scan, an image, an IMU measurement, a robot pose. You can think of the message as the data structure being passed between computational blocks. For example: /odom | | Odometry message v Controller The topic tells us where the data is being communicated. The message tells us what the data looks like . This distinction is important: Topic = communication channel. Message = data carried by the channel. 4. Publishers and subscribers ¶ A node uses a publisher to send messages to a topic. A node uses a subscriber to receive messages from a topic. For example, consider a differential-drive controller. It needs two inputs: The current robot pose. The desired goal. It produces one output: A velocity command. Conceptually: /odom | v +--------------+ | | /goal ->| Controller |-> /cmd_vel | | +--------------+ The controller: subscribes to /odom , subscribes to /goal , computes the control command, publishes to /cmd_vel . A node can have: many inputs and outputs, only inputs, only outputs, or neither. For example, a node that only displays information might only subscribe to topics. A node that generates a fixed command might only publish. 5. Callbacks: where the computation happens ¶ The actual robotics computation still happens in your Python code. ROS 2 does not replace your equations. Suppose your controller uses: heading_error = desired_heading - current_heading and then computes a velocity command. That calculation can be ordinary Python. The difference is how the data gets into and out of the function. In a traditional program: pose = get_pose() goal = get_goal() command = controller(pose, goal) In ROS 2: /odom ----\ \ -> controller callback -> /cmd_vel / /goal ----/ ROS 2 calls the callback when the relevant events occur. This is why ROS 2 is often described as event-driven . 6. Services: request and response ¶ Topics are useful when information is continuously exchanged. But sometimes we want to ask a node to do something and receive a response. That is a service . A useful analogy is: A service is similar to calling a function on another node. For example: reset_simulation() The request might be: "Reset the robot." The response might be: "Reset successful." Unlike a topic, the interaction is explicitly: request | v service | v response Services are useful for short operations where we expect a response. Examples include: resetting a simulator, requesting a calculation, changing a simple state, triggering a short operation. Services are not primarily for starting and stopping nodes . Node lifecycle and process management are handled through other ROS 2 mechanisms. 7. Actions: long-running tasks ¶ What if the request takes a long time? Suppose we tell the robot: "Drive to this goal." The robot might need 30 seconds. A simple service is not ideal because we want to know what is happening while the task is running. An action is designed for this type of problem. An action can provide: a goal, feedback while the goal is executing, a final result, the ability to cancel the goal. Conceptually: goal | v +-------------+ | Action | +-------------+ | feedback | v 20% ... 50% ... 90% | v result For example: "Drive to X = 5, Y = 3." ↓ "Goal accepted." ↓ "30% complete." ↓ "70% complete." ↓ "Goal reached." This makes actions particularly useful for navigation and manipulation tasks. A simple way to remember the three communication patterns is: Topic: exchange information. Service: request something and get a response. Action: request a task that takes time and receive feedback. 8. Parameters: configurable variables ¶ A ROS 2 parameter is a configurable value associated with a node. For example, a controller might have: maximum_speed = 1.0 Kp = 2.0 heading_tolerance = 0.05 Instead of hard-coding these values into the program, we can expose them as ROS parameters. The important idea is: Parameters allow us to configure a node without changing its source code. For example, we might run the same controller with different values of Kp . Parameters are similar to variables in your program, but it is more accurate to think of them as externally configurable settings belonging to a node . 9. Packages: organizing the software ¶ A package is a unit of ROS 2 software organization. A package can contain: Python nodes, Python modules, launch files, configuration files, message definitions, service definitions, action definitions, robot descriptions, other resources. A package might contain one node or many nodes. For example: ddrive package controller node localization node simulator node planner node launch file configuration files The package is therefore closer to a software project than to a single function. 10. Building a package ¶ After creating or modifying ROS 2 software, we commonly use: colcon build The build process prepares the packages in the workspace so they can be used by ROS 2. A useful distinction is: Build = prepare the software. You do not necessarily build only once for the lifetime of a package. You rebuild when you make changes that require rebuilding. For example, adding a package or changing package configuration requires a build. 11. Sourcing a workspace ¶ After building, we commonly run: source install/setup.bash source does not build the package. Instead, it runs the setup script inside your current terminal shell . The setup script changes environment variables so that your terminal knows where your ROS 2 packages, executables, Python modules, and libraries are located. A useful mental model is: Build = prepare the software. Source = tell this terminal where the software is. Run = start the software. You normally need to source the workspace in each new terminal where you want to use that workspace. 12. Running nodes manually ¶ Suppose the ddrive package contains a controller node. After sourcing the workspace, we might run: ros2 run ddrive controller This starts the controller node. If we have several nodes, we could start them individually. For example: ros2 run ddrive localization ros2 run ddrive planner ros2 run ddrive controller ros2 run ddrive simulator This is useful while learning and debugging. However, manually starting a large robot system becomes inconvenient. 13. Launch files ¶ A launch file allows us to start multiple nodes and configure them together. Instead of manually starting: localization planner controller simulator visualization we can create one launch file. Then we can run: ros2 launch ddrive robot.launch.py The launch system starts the required nodes. Conceptually: Launch file | +--------------+--------------+ | | | v v v Localization Planner Controller | v Simulator This is how a real robot system can be started with a single command. Important clarification ¶ You do not need one terminal for every node. You can run multiple processes from a terminal, and launch files can start many nodes for you. The point of a launch file is not simply to avoid opening many terminals. It also lets you specify how the nodes should be configured, which parameters they use, what other resources they need, and how the overall system should start. Putting everything together ¶ Let's return to our differential-drive robot. Suppose we want to drive from a starting point to a goal. We might have: /goal | v +-----------+ | Planner | +-----------+ | /path | v +-----------+ /odom ----> | Controller| ----> /cmd_vel +-----------+ | v +-------------+ | Simulator | +-------------+ | /odom | +----> Controller The important point is that ROS 2 does not provide the robotics equations automatically . Your controller still contains your control law. Your planner still contains your planning algorithm. Your simulator still contains the differential-drive equations. For example, the simulator might integrate: x_dot = v cos(theta) y_dot = v sin(theta) theta_dot = omega ROS 2 provides the software architecture that allows these computational components to communicate. The big picture ¶ Traditional Python programming often looks like: main() | +--> function A | +--> function B | +--> function C ROS 2 turns this into a collection of independent computational components: topic Node A ----------------> Node B | | | | v v topic topic | | +-------> Node C <------+ So the conceptual progression is: Function → a piece of code that performs a computation. Node → an active computational component that stays alive. Callback → a function inside a node that ROS 2 invokes when an event occurs. Topic → a communication channel between nodes. Message → the data traveling through the channel. Service → a request-response interaction. Action → a long-running, feedback-enabled task. Parameter → a configurable value associated with a node. Package → an organized unit of ROS 2 software. Launch file → a way to start and configure a collection of nodes as a system. This gives us the foundation we need for the next step: building the ddrive package and seeing how these concepts become actual Python code.

This is different from a traditional program in which functions are called directly: Traditional Python main() | +--> localization() | +--> planner() | +--> controller() In ROS 2, the components are independent: ROS 2 Localization node ---> topic ---> Controller node | | topic v Simulator node The nodes do not need to directly call one another. They communicate through ROS 2's communication mechanisms.
docs.title: 1. Nodes: active computational blocks

docs.text: The analogy to a function is useful, but a node is not literally a function. A Python ROS 2 node is commonly implemented as a class containing several functions, such as: subscriber callback functions, timer callback functions, service callback functions, action callbacks. The node stays alive, while ROS 2 calls the appropriate function when something happens. For example, a controller might have a callback that executes whenever a new robot pose arrives: new pose arrives | v controller callback() | +--> compute control | +--> publish cmd_vel So a useful mental model is: A node is an active computational block containing functions that respond to events.
docs.title: A node is more than one function

docs.text: A topic is a named communication channel. Topics do not perform the computation themselves. They carry messages between nodes. Think of the analogy with a traditional function: Python function input --> function --> output In ROS 2: Node A --> topic --> Node B The topic is like the connection between the two computational blocks. For example, a localization node might publish the robot's estimated position on the odom topic: Localization node | | publishes pose v /odom | | subscribed by v Controller node The controller does not directly call the localization node. It simply subscribes to /odom . This separation is important because the publisher does not need to know who is listening.
docs.title: 2. Topics: communication channels

docs.text: ROS 2 communication is generally asynchronous. A publisher sends a message when it has one. A subscriber receives it and ROS 2 schedules the appropriate callback. The two nodes do not have to execute at exactly the same time. This is different from a normal Python function call, where the caller waits for the function to execute and return.
docs.title: Topics are asynchronous

docs.text: A message defines the type and structure of data being sent on a topic. For example, a topic might carry: a position, a velocity, a laser scan, an image, an IMU measurement, a robot pose. You can think of the message as the data structure being passed between computational blocks. For example: /odom | | Odometry message v Controller The topic tells us where the data is being communicated. The message tells us what the data looks like . This distinction is important: Topic = communication channel. Message = data carried by the channel.
docs.title: 3. Messages: the data being exchanged

docs.text: A node uses a publisher to send messages to a topic. A node uses a subscriber to receive messages from a topic. For example, consider a differential-drive controller. It needs two inputs: The current robot pose. The desired goal. It produces one output: A velocity command. Conceptually: /odom | v +--------------+ | | /goal ->| Controller |-> /cmd_vel | | +--------------+ The controller: subscribes to /odom , subscribes to /goal , computes the control command, publishes to /cmd_vel . A node can have: many inputs and outputs, only inputs, only outputs, or neither. For example, a node that only displays information might only subscribe to topics. A node that generates a fixed command might only publish.
docs.title: 4. Publishers and subscribers

docs.text: The actual robotics computation still happens in your Python code. ROS 2 does not replace your equations. Suppose your controller uses: heading_error = desired_heading - current_heading and then computes a velocity command. That calculation can be ordinary Python. The difference is how the data gets into and out of the function. In a traditional program: pose = get_pose() goal = get_goal() command = controller(pose, goal) In ROS 2: /odom ----\ \ -> controller callback -> /cmd_vel / /goal ----/ ROS 2 calls the callback when the relevant events occur. This is why ROS 2 is often described as event-driven .
docs.title: 5. Callbacks: where the computation happens

docs.text: Topics are useful when information is continuously exchanged. But sometimes we want to ask a node to do something and receive a response. That is a service . A useful analogy is: A service is similar to calling a function on another node. For example: reset_simulation() The request might be: "Reset the robot." The response might be: "Reset successful." Unlike a topic, the interaction is explicitly: request | v service | v response Services are useful for short operations where we expect a response. Examples include: resetting a simulator, requesting a calculation, changing a simple state, triggering a short operation. Services are not primarily for starting and stopping nodes . Node lifecycle and process management are handled through other ROS 2 mechanisms.
docs.title: 6. Services: request and response

docs.text: What if the request takes a long time? Suppose we tell the robot: "Drive to this goal." The robot might need 30 seconds. A simple service is not ideal because we want to know what is happening while the task is running. An action is designed for this type of problem. An action can provide: a goal, feedback while the goal is executing, a final result, the ability to cancel the goal. Conceptually: goal | v +-------------+ | Action | +-------------+ | feedback | v 20% ... 50% ... 90% | v result For example: "Drive to X = 5, Y = 3." ↓ "Goal accepted." ↓ "30% complete." ↓ "70% complete." ↓ "Goal reached." This makes actions particularly useful for navigation and manipulation tasks. A simple way to remember the three communication patterns is: Topic: exchange information. Service: request something and get a response. Action: request a task that takes time and receive feedback.
docs.title: 7. Actions: long-running tasks

docs.text: A ROS 2 parameter is a configurable value associated with a node. For example, a controller might have: maximum_speed = 1.0 Kp = 2.0 heading_tolerance = 0.05 Instead of hard-coding these values into the program, we can expose them as ROS parameters. The important idea is: Parameters allow us to configure a node without changing its source code. For example, we might run the same controller with different values of Kp . Parameters are similar to variables in your program, but it is more accurate to think of them as externally configurable settings belonging to a node .
docs.title: 8. Parameters: configurable variables

docs.text: A package is a unit of ROS 2 software organization. A package can contain: Python nodes, Python modules, launch files, configuration files, message definitions, service definitions, action definitions, robot descriptions, other resources. A package might contain one node or many nodes. For example: ddrive package controller node localization node simulator node planner node launch file configuration files The package is therefore closer to a software project than to a single function.
docs.title: 9. Packages: organizing the software

docs.text: After creating or modifying ROS 2 software, we commonly use: colcon build The build process prepares the packages in the workspace so they can be used by ROS 2. A useful distinction is: Build = prepare the software. You do not necessarily build only once for the lifetime of a package. You rebuild when you make changes that require rebuilding. For example, adding a package or changing package configuration requires a build.
docs.title: 10. Building a package

docs.text: After building, we commonly run: source install/setup.bash source does not build the package. Instead, it runs the setup script inside your current terminal shell . The setup script changes environment variables so that your terminal knows where your ROS 2 packages, executables, Python modules, and libraries are located. A useful mental model is: Build = prepare the software. Source = tell this terminal where the software is. Run = start the software. You normally need to source the workspace in each new terminal where you want to use that workspace.
docs.title: 11. Sourcing a workspace

docs.text: Suppose the ddrive package contains a controller node. After sourcing the workspace, we might run: ros2 run ddrive controller This starts the controller node. If we have several nodes, we could start them individually. For example: ros2 run ddrive localization ros2 run ddrive planner ros2 run ddrive controller ros2 run ddrive simulator This is useful while learning and debugging. However, manually starting a large robot system becomes inconvenient.
docs.title: 12. Running nodes manually

docs.text: A launch file allows us to start multiple nodes and configure them together. Instead of manually starting: localization planner controller simulator visualization we can create one launch file. Then we can run: ros2 launch ddrive robot.launch.py The launch system starts the required nodes. Conceptually: Launch file | +--------------+--------------+ | | | v v v Localization Planner Controller | v Simulator This is how a real robot system can be started with a single command.
docs.title: 13. Launch files

docs.text: You do not need one terminal for every node. You can run multiple processes from a terminal, and launch files can start many nodes for you. The point of a launch file is not simply to avoid opening many terminals. It also lets you specify how the nodes should be configured, which parameters they use, what other resources they need, and how the overall system should start.
docs.title: Important clarification

docs.text: Let's return to our differential-drive robot. Suppose we want to drive from a starting point to a goal. We might have: /goal | v +-----------+ | Planner | +-----------+ | /path | v +-----------+ /odom ----> | Controller| ----> /cmd_vel +-----------+ | v +-------------+ | Simulator | +-------------+ | /odom | +----> Controller The important point is that ROS 2 does not provide the robotics equations automatically . Your controller still contains your control law. Your planner still contains your planning algorithm. Your simulator still contains the differential-drive equations. For example, the simulator might integrate: x_dot = v cos(theta) y_dot = v sin(theta) theta_dot = omega ROS 2 provides the software architecture that allows these computational components to communicate.
docs.title: Putting everything together

docs.text: Traditional Python programming often looks like: main() | +--> function A | +--> function B | +--> function C ROS 2 turns this into a collection of independent computational components: topic Node A ----------------> Node B | | | | v v topic topic | | +-------> Node C <------+ So the conceptual progression is: Function → a piece of code that performs a computation. Node → an active computational component that stays alive. Callback → a function inside a node that ROS 2 invokes when an event occurs. Topic → a communication channel between nodes. Message → the data traveling through the channel. Service → a request-response interaction. Action → a long-running, feedback-enabled task. Parameter → a configurable value associated with a node. Package → an organized unit of ROS 2 software. Launch file → a way to start and configure a collection of nodes as a system. This gives us the foundation we need for the next step: building the ddrive package and seeing how these concepts become actual Python code.
docs.title: The big picture

docs.text: 2.2 ddrive: Forward Kinematics ¶ Package download Download ddrive.zip ddrive is a two-node "turtlesim, but you built it" package. One node holds a pose and integrates it with a hand-written Euler integrator; the other node visualizes it. Node Owns Subscribes Publishes ddrive_sim the pose [x, y, theta] , the integrator /cmd_vel ( geometry_msgs/Twist ) /pose ( geometry_msgs/Pose2D ) ddrive_viz nothing — just draws /pose — (opens a matplotlib window) ddrive_sim works fine with nobody ever publishing to /cmd_vel — it just holds still at its initial pose and keeps publishing that pose every dt seconds. That's what makes the staged workflow below possible: you can see the system before you drive it. 0. Install the package ¶ mkdir -p ~/ros2_ws/src cp -r ddrive ~/ros2_ws/src/ cd ~/ros2_ws source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y colcon build --packages-select ddrive source install/setup.bash Checkpoint: ros2 pkg executables ddrive should list exactly two: ddrive ddrive_sim and ddrive ddrive_viz . 1. What's in the package ¶ ddrive/ ├── package.xml # name, dependencies (rclpy, geometry_msgs), build type ├── setup.py # registers the two executables below ├── setup.cfg ├── resource/ddrive # marker file ament needs to find the package ├── config/ │ └── params.yaml # default parameters for both nodes ├── launch/ │ └── ddrive_launch.py # brings sim + viz up together └── ddrive/ ├── __init__.py ├── kinematics.py # pure Python, no ROS import — the Euler integrator ├── sim_node.py # ddrive_sim └── viz_node.py # ddrive_viz kinematics.py is deliberately ROS-free. It's the same math as the original diff_drive_fk.py script's euler_integration() function, just refactored into a euler_step(z, u, dt) function: def euler_step ( z , u , dt ): x0 , y0 , theta0 = z v , omega = u xdot = v * math . cos ( theta0 ) ydot = v * math . sin ( theta0 ) thetadot = omega x1 = x0 + xdot * dt y1 = y0 + ydot * dt theta1 = theta0 + thetadot * dt return [ x1 , y1 , theta1 ] sim_node.py wraps that in ROS: a subscriber updates the commanded [v, omega] whenever /cmd_vel arrives, and a separate timer calls euler_step every dt seconds using whatever the latest command was: def _cmd_vel_cb ( self , msg : Twist ): self . _u = [ msg . linear . x , msg . angular . z ] # just caches it def _step ( self ): # runs every dt seconds self . _z = euler_step ( self . _z , self . _u , self . _dt ) ... publish self . _z as Pose2D on 'pose' ... There's no loop connecting these two — rclpy.spin() 's executor calls whichever callback is ready (a new message, or the timer firing) and that's the whole "cycle." viz_node.py subscribes to /pose and redraws on every message, same circle-plus-heading-line drawing as the original script's animate() , just triggered by messages instead of a precomputed array. 2. Run it ¶ Stage 1 — pose, no motion (2 terminals) ¶ Terminal 1: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive ddrive_sim Override the initial pose to prove it's a real parameter, not hard-coded: ros2 run ddrive ddrive_sim --ros-args -p x0: = 1 .0 -p y0: = -0.5 -p theta0: = 1 .5708 Terminal 2: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive ddrive_viz A matplotlib window opens with the robot sitting still at whatever pose you set in Terminal 1. Stage 2 — command it (3rd terminal) ¶ Keep Terminals 1–2 running. Terminal 3: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.3}, angular: {z: 0.2}}" -r 10 Watch the plot window — the robot curves immediately. Ctrl+C, then stop it properly (it keeps the last command it received otherwise): ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.0}, angular: {z: 0.0}}" -1 When you Ctrl+C ddrive_viz , it saves the trail to ddrive_trajectory.png in its working directory. Stage 3 — collapse into a launch file ¶ ros2 launch ddrive ddrive_launch.py Same two nodes, one command. Overridable arguments: ros2 launch ddrive ddrive_launch.py x0: = 1 .0 theta0: = 1 .5708 dt: = 0 .05 robot_radius: = 0 .3 3. Look at the graph — nodes and topics ¶ With sim + viz running: ros2 node list ros2 node info /ddrive_sim ros2 topic list ros2 topic info /cmd_vel --verbose ros2 topic echo /pose ros2 topic hz /pose node info on /ddrive_sim shows it subscribing to /cmd_vel and publishing /pose . If rqt_graph is installed, this draws the same picture live: rqt_graph 4. Change how fast it moves ¶ Any of these on /cmd_vel changes the motion in real time (with ddrive_sim + ddrive_viz running): # straight line ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.5}}" -r 10 # spin in place ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{angular: {z: 1.0}}" -r 10 # arc ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.4}, angular: {z: 0.5}}" -r 10 -r 10 repeats at 10 Hz; -1 publishes once and exits. 5. Parameters — more than one way to set them ¶ Using robot_radius (a ddrive_viz parameter) as the running example: Code default , in viz_node.py : self . declare_parameter ( 'robot_radius' , 0.1 ) CLI override at startup: ros2 run ddrive ddrive_viz --ros-args -p robot_radius: = 0 .2 YAML file ( config/params.yaml , installed to the package share dir): ddrive_viz : ros__parameters : robot_radius : 0.2 axis_limit : 2.0 save_path : ddrive_trajectory.png ros2 run ddrive ddrive_viz --ros-args --params-file \ ~/ros2_ws/install/ddrive/share/ddrive/config/params.yaml Launch argument: ros2 launch ddrive ddrive_launch.py robot_radius: = 0 .3 Live, while the node is running — this needs the node to register a callback, or ros2 param set silently changes the stored value without changing behavior: self . add_on_set_parameters_callback ( self . _on_param_change ) def _on_param_change ( self , params ): for p in params : if p . name == 'robot_radius' : self . _R = p . value # ... return SetParametersResult ( successful = True ) ros2 param get /ddrive_viz robot_radius ros2 param set /ddrive_viz robot_radius 0 .4 ddrive_viz has this callback wired up, so the circle resizes on the next redraw. ddrive_sim 's dt does not have one — try ros2 param set /ddrive_sim dt 0.02 and notice the timer's rate doesn't actually change. Worth demonstrating both, back to back. 6. What's next ¶ ddrive_ik builds directly on top of this package — same ddrive_sim and ddrive_viz , unmodified, with two new nodes added to close a tracking control loop. See the next page. ddrive_sim also now has a ResetPose service — see Part 3 of the ddrive_ik_msgs page for the server code, the terminal client, and how to call it.

docs.text: 2.3 ddrive_ik: Trajectory Tracking ¶ Package download Download ddrive_ik.zip ddrive_ik adds trajectory tracking on top of ddrive — it does not duplicate ddrive_sim or ddrive_viz , it depends on them. Node Package Subscribes Publishes ddrive_sim ddrive /cmd_vel /pose ddrive_viz ddrive /pose — ddrive_trajectory ddrive_ik — /reference ddrive_controller ddrive_ik /pose , /reference /cmd_vel 0. Install (build order matters here) ¶ Both packages need to be in the same workspace, and ddrive needs to build first since ddrive_ik depends on it: cp -r ddrive ~/ros2_ws/src/ # if not already there cp -r ddrive_ik ~/ros2_ws/src/ cd ~/ros2_ws source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -r -y colcon build --packages-select ddrive ddrive_ik source install/setup.bash colcon figures out the build order itself from ddrive_ik/package.xml declaring ddrive as an exec_depend — you don't have to specify it. Checkpoint: ros2 pkg executables ddrive_ik should list ddrive_ik ddrive_trajectory and ddrive_ik ddrive_controller . 1. What's new here ¶ ddrive_ik/ ├── package.xml # exec_depend on rclpy, geometry_msgs, AND ddrive ├── setup.py ├── config/ │ ├── params.yaml # this package's own two nodes │ └── tracking_params.yaml # all three timed nodes, including ddrive_sim ├── launch/ │ └── tracking_launch.py # starts nodes from BOTH ddrive and ddrive_ik └── ddrive_ik/ ├── kinematics.py # point-offset transforms + control law ├── trajectories.py # astroid / circle reference curves ├── trajectory_node.py # ddrive_trajectory └── controller_node.py # ddrive_controller This is a different kinematics.py than the one in ddrive — that one has the forward-kinematics integrator; this one has the tracking control law. They're never ambiguous because the package name is part of the import path: ddrive.kinematics vs. ddrive_ik.kinematics . 2. Run it ¶ Terminal by terminal (4 terminals) ¶ The robot needs to start where the reference curve starts, or the controller's first correction is huge (see the debugging note below). For the default astroid ( scale=1.0, px=0.05, py=0.0 ), that start point is x0=0.95, y0=0.0, theta0=0.0 . Terminal 1 — simulator, seeded to match the curve: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive ddrive_sim --ros-args -p x0: = 0 .95 -p y0: = 0 .0 -p theta0: = 0 .0 -p dt: = 0 .01 Terminal 2 — visualizer: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive ddrive_viz Terminal 3 — trajectory generator: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive_ik ddrive_trajectory --ros-args -p dt: = 0 .01 Nothing moves yet — confirm it's publishing: ros2 topic echo /reference Terminal 4 — controller: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive_ik ddrive_controller --ros-args -p dt: = 0 .01 The robot should ease onto the astroid and trace it continuously, looping every 10 seconds. Collapsed into one launch file ¶ ros2 launch ddrive_ik tracking_launch.py No arguments needed — the seeded start pose and dt=0.01 are already the defaults. Try other shapes/gains: ros2 launch ddrive_ik tracking_launch.py shape: = circle period: = 6 .0 ros2 launch ddrive_ik tracking_launch.py Kp: = 20 .0 If you change scale , px , or py , recompute the seed pose: x0 = scale - px , y0 = -py , theta0 = 0 (the curve always starts at point P = (scale, 0) at t=0 ). 3. The control law is designed so the tracking error decays as edot ≈ -Kp · e in continuous time. Euler-discretized at step dt , that becomes: e[n+1] = e[n] · (1 - Kp·dt) This only decays if 0 < Kp·dt < 2 . docs.text: 2.4 ddrive_ik_msgs: Services & Actions ¶ Package download Download ddrive_ik_msgs.zip Everything so far — ddrive and ddrive_ik — communicates entirely through topics: /pose , /cmd_vel , /reference . Topics are one of three ways ROS 2 nodes talk to each other. This page covers the other two, in three parts: the concepts, the interface definitions, and then the actual service/action code wired into ddrive and ddrive_ik . Part 1 — Concepts: topics vs. services vs. actions ¶ Topic (what you've used) Service Action Pattern publish/subscribe request → response goal → feedback → result Who talks to whom many-to-many one client, one server one client, one server Blocking? never — fire and forget client waits for the response client gets progress updates, doesn't block Duration ongoing stream fast, bounded (milliseconds) can take a long time Cancelable mid-way? n/a no yes Feedback while running? n/a no yes Real-world example /cmd_vel , /pose "add two ints", "reset the map" "navigate to this pose" (nav2) The intuition: topics are for continuous state that keeps flowing whether or not anyone's listening. Services are for "ask a quick, well-defined question, get one answer" — a function call over the network. Actions are for "start a task that takes a while, tell me how it's going, let me cancel it" — and are actually built on top of services and topics under the hood (a goal service, a cancel service, a result service, plus a feedback topic and a status topic). Beginner vs. Intermediate The official ROS 2 tutorials cover services in the Beginner series, right after topics. Actions are Intermediate . If you're following the tutorials in order, services come next; actions are a reasonable stretch beyond that, not a beginner-series gap. Where these fit into this course: ResetPose (service) — snaps ddrive_sim 's pose to a given (x, y, theta) instantly. A service fits because resetting has a definite, immediate answer ("done" or "failed") — the same shape as "add two ints," just for this robot. TrackTrajectory (action) — track the reference curve for a bounded number of loops, with feedback (loops completed, current error) published as it runs, and a result (total time, final error) when it finishes — cancelable mid-run. This is the first place in the course where a topic-only design genuinely falls short: ddrive_controller tracks forever, with no way to say "and stop after this" or "how's it going so far." Part 2 — The interface definitions ¶ Every node so far is an ament_python package. Generating real message classes from .srv / .action files requires rosidl_generate_interfaces , which only runs inside an ament_cmake package — a hard ROS 2 constraint, not a style choice. So ddrive_ik_msgs exists purely to hold these two definitions; it has no Python code, no nodes, nothing to ros2 run on its own. ddrive_ik_msgs/ ├── package.xml # ament_cmake, not ament_python ├── CMakeLists.txt # calls rosidl_generate_interfaces ├── srv/ │ └── ResetPose.srv └── action/ └── TrackTrajectory.action ResetPose.srv — request above --- , response below: float64 x float64 y float64 theta --- bool success string message TrackTrajectory.action — three blocks: goal, result, feedback: int32 num_loops --- float64 total_time float64 final_error --- int32 loops_completed float64 current_error CMakeLists.txt : cmake_minimum_required ( VERSION 3.8 ) project ( ddrive_ik_msgs ) find_package ( ament_cmake REQUIRED ) find_package ( rosidl_default_generators REQUIRED ) rosidl_generate_interfaces ( ${ PROJECT_NAME } "srv/ResetPose.srv" "action/TrackTrajectory.action" ) ament_package () Build it on its own first, before wiring anything to it: cp -r ddrive_ik_msgs ~/ros2_ws/src/ cd ~/ros2_ws source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash colcon build --packages-select ddrive_ik_msgs source install/setup.bash Checkpoint: ros2 interface show ddrive_ik_msgs/srv/ResetPose ros2 interface show ddrive_ik_msgs/action/TrackTrajectory Part 3 — Using them: ResetPose (ddrive) and TrackTrajectory (ddrive_ik) ¶ Both ddrive and ddrive_ik now depend on ddrive_ik_msgs — the same exec_depend pattern ddrive_ik already used for ddrive , just one more package added to the graph: <exec_depend> ddrive_ik_msgs </exec_depend> ResetPose — service server in ddrive_sim ¶ The server lives in ddrive_sim (package ddrive ) because that's the node that actually owns the pose state z . The callback just overwrites it and reports success: from ddrive_ik_msgs.srv import ResetPose self . create_service ( ResetPose , 'reset_pose' , self . _reset_pose_cb ) def _reset_pose_cb ( self , request , response ): self . _z = [ request . x , request . y , request . theta ] response . success = True response . message = f 'pose reset to x= { request . x } , y= { request . y } , theta= { request . theta } ' return response Get ddrive_sim running first — /reset_pose only exists while that node is up. Easiest way is the launch file from the ddrive page , which brings up ddrive_sim + ddrive_viz together: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 launch ddrive ddrive_launch.py (Two separate ros2 run terminals for ddrive_sim and ddrive_viz work just as well, if you'd rather see them as separate processes — see Stage 1 on the ddrive page .) Checkpoint before calling the service — confirm it actually exists: ros2 service list | grep reset_pose With that running, a small client, ddrive_reset_pose_client , calls it once and exits — unlike a node, a service client doesn't need an ongoing relationship with anything: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive ddrive_reset_pose_client 0 .95 0 .0 0 .0 Watch the plot window jump to (0.95, 0) the instant the client call returns. You can also call it directly from the CLI, no client code needed: ros2 service call /reset_pose ddrive_ik_msgs/srv/ResetPose "{x: 0.0, y: 0.0, theta: 0.0}" TrackTrajectory — action server in ddrive_ik ¶ This one lives in a new node , ddrive_track_action_server , in ddrive_ik — deliberately not folded into ddrive_controller . The action server only watches /pose and /reference (the same topics ddrive_controller already uses) and reports progress; it never publishes /cmd_vel itself. ddrive_controller keeps tracking forever regardless of whether any action goal is active — the action just adds a bounded, observable "session" on top of that endless process: self . _action_server = ActionServer ( self , TrackTrajectory , 'track_trajectory' , execute_callback = self . _execute_cb , goal_callback = self . _goal_cb , cancel_callback = self . _cancel_cb , ) def _execute_cb ( self , goal_handle ): num_loops = goal_handle . request . num_loops total_duration = num_loops * self . _period start = time . monotonic () while ( time . monotonic () - start ) < total_duration : if goal_handle . is_cancel_requested : goal_handle . canceled () ... # return an early Result feedback . loops_completed = int (( time . monotonic () - start ) // self . _period ) feedback . current_error = self . _current_error () goal_handle . publish_feedback ( feedback ) time . sleep ( 0.5 ) goal_handle . succeed () ... # return the final Result Why MultiThreadedExecutor _execute_cb blocks on time.sleep() while polling for cancellation. With the default single-threaded executor, a cancel request would never get processed while that sleep is happening — so main() spins this node with a MultiThreadedExecutor instead, matching the official rclpy action tutorial's guidance. Get everything running first — the action server needs /pose and /reference actually flowing (from ddrive_sim and ddrive_trajectory ) to report a meaningful current_error , and ddrive_controller needs to be running for the robot to actually move. tracking_launch.py now starts all five nodes together, including ddrive_track_action_server : source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 launch ddrive_ik tracking_launch.py (Terminal-by-terminal works too, if you'd rather see each node start separately — see Run it, terminal by terminal on the ddrive_ik page , then add a 5th terminal for ddrive_track_action_server on top of those four.) Checkpoint before sending a goal — confirm the action actually exists: ros2 action list should include /track_trajectory . With that running, the client, ddrive_track_action_client , sends a goal, prints feedback as it streams in, and sends a cancel request on Ctrl+C instead of just quitting: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive_ik ddrive_track_action_client 2 This should print a feedback: line roughly every half second showing loops_completed climbing and current_error fluctuating as the robot tracks, then a result: line once 2 full loops complete. Ctrl+C partway through and confirm the action server's terminal logs goal canceled instead of goal succeeded . You can also send a goal without any client code: ros2 action send_goal /track_trajectory ddrive_ik_msgs/action/TrackTrajectory "{num_loops: 1}" --feedback Build both packages with the new dependency ¶ cd ~/ros2_ws rm -rf build/ddrive build/ddrive_ik install/ddrive install/ddrive_ik log source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash colcon build --packages-select ddrive ddrive_ik source install/setup.bash

docs.text: This one lives in a new node , ddrive_track_action_server , in ddrive_ik — deliberately not folded into ddrive_controller . The action server only watches /pose and /reference (the same topics ddrive_controller already uses) and reports progress; it never publishes /cmd_vel itself. ddrive_controller keeps tracking forever regardless of whether any action goal is active — the action just adds a bounded, observable "session" on top of that endless process: self . _action_server = ActionServer ( self , TrackTrajectory , 'track_trajectory' , execute_callback = self . _execute_cb , goal_callback = self . _goal_cb , cancel_callback = self . _cancel_cb , ) def _execute_cb ( self , goal_handle ): num_loops = goal_handle . request . num_loops total_duration = num_loops * self . _period start = time . monotonic () while ( time . monotonic () - start ) < total_duration : if goal_handle . is_cancel_requested : goal_handle . canceled () ... # return an early Result feedback . loops_completed = int (( time . monotonic () - start ) // self . _period ) feedback . current_error = self . _current_error () goal_handle . publish_feedback ( feedback ) time . sleep ( 0.5 ) goal_handle . succeed () ... # return the final Result Why MultiThreadedExecutor _execute_cb blocks on time.sleep() while polling for cancellation. With the default single-threaded executor, a cancel request would never get processed while that sleep is happening — so main() spins this node with a MultiThreadedExecutor instead, matching the official rclpy action tutorial's guidance. Get everything running first — the action server needs /pose and /reference actually flowing (from ddrive_sim and ddrive_trajectory ) to report a meaningful current_error , and ddrive_controller needs to be running for the robot to actually move. tracking_launch.py now starts all five nodes together, including ddrive_track_action_server : source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 launch ddrive_ik tracking_launch.py (Terminal-by-terminal works too, if you'd rather see each node start separately — see Run it, terminal by terminal on the ddrive_ik page , then add a 5th terminal for ddrive_track_action_server on top of those four.) Checkpoint before sending a goal — confirm the action actually exists: ros2 action list should include /track_trajectory . With that running, the client, ddrive_track_action_client , sends a goal, prints feedback as it streams in, and sends a cancel request on Ctrl+C instead of just quitting: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 run ddrive_ik ddrive_track_action_client 2 This should print a feedback: line roughly every half second showing loops_completed climbing and current_error fluctuating as the robot tracks, then a result: line once 2 full loops complete. Ctrl+C partway through and confirm the action server's terminal logs goal canceled instead of goal succeeded . You can also send a goal without any client code: ros2 action send_goal /track_trajectory ddrive_ik_msgs/action/TrackTrajectory "{num_loops: 1}" --feedback

docs.text: 2.5 Exercise: Mecanum Car ¶ Now that you've built ddrive , ddrive_ik , and ddrive_ik_msgs for a differential-drive (unicycle) robot, repeat the exercise for a mecanum-wheel car — a holonomic robot that can move in any direction without needing to rotate first. The model ¶ ddrive 's unicycle model couples heading and motion — the robot can only move along the direction it's currently facing: xdot = v * cos(theta) ydot = v * sin(theta) thetadot = omega A mecanum (holonomic) drive decouples them. For this exercise, use the simplified model: xdot = vx ydot = vy where vx and vy are commanded velocities in the world frame, independent of any heading. (If you want to go further, add a theta state and thetadot = omega back in, and decide for yourself whether vx / vy should be interpreted in the world frame or the robot's body frame — mecanum wheels genuinely support both, and the difference is a good thing to reason through.) What to build ¶ Mirror the ddrive package structure: ddrive_mecanum/ ├── package.xml ├── setup.py ├── setup.cfg ├── resource/ddrive_mecanum ├── config/ │ └── params.yaml ├── launch/ │ └── ddrive_mecanum_launch.py └── ddrive_mecanum/ ├── __init__.py ├── kinematics.py # your new xdot=vx, ydot=vy integrator ├── sim_node.py # subscribes /cmd_vel, integrates, publishes /pose └── viz_node.py # same matplotlib visualization as ddrive_viz /cmd_vel is still a geometry_msgs/Twist — just interpret linear.x / linear.y as vx / vy instead of linear.x / angular.z as v / omega . Suggested steps ¶ Kinematics first, no ROS. Write and test euler_step(z, u, dt) for the new model as a plain Python function, same as ddrive 's kinematics.py — verify it moves diagonally when vx and vy are both nonzero, and that it's genuinely decoupled from heading. Wrap it in a node. Copy sim_node.py from ddrive and swap in the new kinematics. Reuse the visualizer. ddrive_viz 's drawing code barely needs to change — a circle plus a heading line still works, even if heading is now cosmetic rather than driving the motion. Drive it. Command diagonal, sideways, and combined motions and confirm the robot actually moves in directions a unicycle robot couldn't reach without turning first: ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.3, y: 0.3}}" -r 10 Collapse into a launch file , same pattern as ddrive_launch.py . Stretch goals ¶ Add ddrive_ik -style trajectory tracking on top: pick a reference curve and a control law that works for a fully decoupled (x, y) system — it should end up simpler than the point-offset feedback-linearization trick ddrive_ik needed, since there's no heading coupling to work around. Add the theta / omega state back in and support commanding heading independently of translation. Add a ResetPose service, same pattern as ddrive_ik_msgs . Deliverables ¶ [ ] kinematics.py with a working euler_step for the new model [ ] sim_node.py + viz_node.py running and visibly moving [ ] A launch file that brings both up together [ ] A short write-up (a few sentences) of what changed vs. ddrive and why — this is the point of the exercise, not just working code

docs.text: 3.3 Exercise: threelink_ik ¶ Extend twolink_ik to a three-link planar arm. The new wrinkle: you're no longer just solving for a target position — you're also solving for the end-effector's orientation . The model ¶ For a two-link planar arm, twolink_ik solves 2 equations ( x_ref , y_ref ) for 2 unknowns ( theta1 , theta2 ) — exactly determined. Add a third link and the forward kinematics becomes: x = l1*cos(theta1) + l2*cos(theta1+theta2) + l3*cos(theta1+theta2+theta3) y = l1*sin(theta1) + l2*sin(theta1+theta2) + l3*sin(theta1+theta2+theta3) phi = theta1 + theta2 + theta3 phi — the end-effector's orientation relative to the world x-axis — falls out for free from a serial planar chain: it's just the sum of all the joint angles. That gives you a third equation, which is exactly what you need for a third unknown: with 3 links you now solve 3 equations ( x_ref , y_ref , phi_ref ) for 3 unknowns ( theta1 , theta2 , theta3 ) — still exactly determined, same as twolink_ik was with 2 and 2. For this exercise, fix the target orientation at: phi_ref = 90° (pi/2 rad) — end effector pointing straight up What to build ¶ Mirror the twolink_ik package structure: threelink_ik/ ├── urdf/ │ └── threelink.urdf.xacro # joint1, joint2, joint3; l1, l2, l3 as xacro args ├── config/ │ └── threelink_ik_params.yaml # l1, l2, l3, x_ref, y_ref, phi_ref ├── launch/ │ └── threelink_ik.launch.py # robot_state_publisher + ik_node + rviz ├── rviz/ │ └── threelink_ik.rviz └── threelink_ik/ ├── kinematics.py # forward_kinematics() + inverse_kinematics() └── ik_node.py # loads l1, l2, l3, x_ref, y_ref, phi_ref -> solves once -> publishes /joint_states Suggested steps ¶ Extend the URDF. Add a third revolute joint and link, same pattern as joint1 / joint2 in twolink 's xacro — just chained one further. Extend forward_kinematics() . Add the l3 / theta3 terms to x , y , and add the new phi = theta1 + theta2 + theta3 output. Extend the fsolve residual. twolink_ik 's residual function returns [x - x_ref, y - y_ref] ; yours needs a third entry, [x - x_ref, y - y_ref, phi - phi_ref] , and fsolve now solves for [theta1, theta2, theta3] instead of [theta1, theta2] . Set the target in config/threelink_ik_params.yaml : /** : ros__parameters : l1 : 1.0 l2 : 1.0 l3 : 0.5 x_ref : 0.8 y_ref : 0.8 phi_ref : 1.5708 # 90 degrees, in radians Verify with tf2 , same trick as twolink_ik : ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo base_link end_effector The translation should match (x_ref, y_ref, 0) — but this time, also check the rotation. end_effector 's frame should show a rotation of phi_ref about Z. Things worth thinking about ¶ With phi_ref fixed, does every (x_ref, y_ref) you try actually have a solution? (Hint: think about the arm's total reach, and what configurations can hold the end effector vertical while still reaching a given point — not every point in the two-link arm's reachable set is still reachable once orientation is constrained.) fsolve needs an initial guess. If it fails to converge or lands on a physically odd (e.g. self-intersecting) configuration, try a different starting guess — same lesson as any nonlinear solver, just more visible with a third joint added. Deliverables ¶ [ ] threelink.urdf.xacro with three working revolute joints [ ] kinematics.py with forward_kinematics() returning (x, y, phi) and inverse_kinematics() solving all three joint angles [ ] ik_node.py publishing /joint_states so RViz shows the arm reaching (x_ref, y_ref) with the end effector vertical [ ] tf2 check confirming both position and orientation match target

docs.text: 4.1 dbpendulum ¶ Package download Download dbpendulum.zip Double (two-link) pendulum for ROS2 Jazzy: no controller, real mass/inertia, Gazebo Sim physics, chaotic motion. Unlike twolink / twolink_ik , the joint angles here are not commanded — Gazebo's physics engine integrates the dynamics itself, and robot_state_publisher /RViz just display the result. Install prerequisite ¶ sudo apt update sudo apt install ros-jazzy-ros-gz Pulls in ros_gz_sim and ros_gz_bridge in one shot. Build ¶ Terminal 1: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash cd ~/ros2_ws colcon build --packages-select dbpendulum --symlink-install Run ¶ Terminal 1: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 launch dbpendulum dbpendulum.launch.py This starts Gazebo Sim (running, not paused), spawns the pendulum, and opens RViz. The view is already framed on a front (X-Z plane) camera angle, and the pendulum starts just past its inverted, unstable equilibrium — gravity takes over immediately and it swings chaotically without any input. Parameters ¶ Set in config/dbpendulum_params.yaml , passed into the URDF as xacro args. They match the parameters class in the course's main_double_pendulum.py reference script: Param Meaning Default m1 link 1 mass 1.0 m2 link 2 mass 1.0 I1 link 1 moment of inertia about its own COM 0.1 I2 link 2 moment of inertia about its own COM 0.1 c1 pivot-to-COM distance, link 1 0.5 c2 pivot-to-COM distance, link 2 0.5 l link length 1.0 Design notes ¶ Real <inertial> tags. docs.text: 4.2 dbpendulum_ctrl ¶ Package download Download dbpendulum_ctrl.zip Same double pendulum as 4.1 dbpendulum , now actuated: a feedback-linearization (computed-torque) controller tracks a point-to-point reference trajectory, emulating the course's 4b_doublependulum_trajectory_tracking/twoink_main.py reference script. Unlike dbpendulum , motion here is commanded, not passive — the pendulum starts at rest and smoothly moves through a planned trajectory instead of swinging chaotically under gravity alone. Install prerequisite ¶ sudo apt update sudo apt install ros-jazzy-ros-gz sudo apt install ros-jazzy-ros2-control ros-jazzy-ros2-controllers ros-jazzy-gz-ros2-control The first line is the same Gazebo/ROS2 bridge dbpendulum needs. The second adds ros2_control and gz_ros2_control , which this package uses to send torque (effort) commands into Gazebo — dbpendulum never needed these, since it has no actuation at all. Build ¶ Terminal 1: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash cd ~/ros2_ws colcon build --packages-select dbpendulum_ctrl --symlink-install Run ¶ Terminal 1: source /opt/ros/ $ROS_DISTRO /setup.bash source ~/ros2_ws/install/setup.bash ros2 launch dbpendulum_ctrl dbpendulum_ctrl.launch.py This starts Gazebo Sim, spawns the pendulum already at the trajectory's start pose, brings up ros2_control 's controller manager, and starts the control node. Link1 sweeps through a 1-rad move over 3s while link2 swings out and back over two 1.5s segments — all driven by torques computed live from the feedback-linearization law, not by directly setting joint angles. Parameters ¶ Set in config/dbpendulum_ctrl_params.yaml . The physical parameters ( m1 ... l ) describe the same physical robot as dbpendulum 's dbpendulum_params.yaml ; g and the gains are specific to this package: Param Meaning Default m1 link 1 mass 1.0 m2 link 2 mass 1.0 I1 link 1 moment of inertia about its own COM 0.1 I2 link 2 moment of inertia about its own COM 0.1 c1 pivot-to-COM distance, link 1 0.5 c2 pivot-to-COM distance, link 2 0.5 l link length 1.0 g gravity used inside the controller's model 9.8 kp1 , kp2 proportional gain, joint 1 / joint 2 100.0 kd1 , kd2 derivative gain, joint 1 / joint 2 20.0 ( 2*sqrt(kp) , critically damped) Design notes ¶ Feedback linearization, ported directly. The control node computes T = M(theta)*(qddot_ref - Kp*(theta-theta_ref) - Kd*(thetadot-thetadot_ref)) + C(theta,thetadot) + G(theta) using the exact same M11/M12/M21/M22/C1/C2/G1/G2 closed-form expressions as twoink_main.py 's control() function. Because the model terms cancel the plant's actual dynamics exactly, the tracking error settles into a simple critically-damped linear response — verified in a standalone (non-ROS2) simulation with tracking error under 1e-6 rad. g is 9.8, not the reference script's illustrative 10. Feedback linearization only cancels gravity/Coriolis/inertia exactly if the controller's internal model matches the actual simulated plant — so this tracks Gazebo's real default gravity, same as dbpendulum . A different joint convention than dbpendulum , on purpose. The reference script's dynamics are derived in a planar (x, y-up, theta measured from the +x axis) convention. Rather than bolt a hand-derived offset/sign correction onto dbpendulum 's "hangs down along -Z" geometry, this package's URDF uses a different axis and link direction ( axis="0 -1 0" , links extending along local +X) chosen so the raw joint angle is theta1 / theta2 in the script's exact sense, offset zero. This package's URDF is not interchangeable with dbpendulum 's. No JointStatePublisher gz-sim plugin, no /joint_states bridge. joint_state_broadcaster (a ros2_control controller) publishes /joint_states as a native ROS2 topic directly from the hardware state interfaces. The only gz-transport↔ROS2 bridge left is /clock . Torque commands go through a plain pass-through controller. effort_controller ( forward_command_controller/ForwardCommandController , interface_name: effort ) does no control of its own — it just forwards the control node's [T1, T2] published on /effort_controller/commands straight to the joints. All the actual control law lives in the dbpendulum_ctrl node, not in a canned ros2_control controller. Initial condition must match the trajectory's t=0 . The URDF's <ros2_control> block sets each joint's initial_value to the trajectory's starting angles ( theta1(0) = -pi/2 - 0.5 , theta2(0) = 0 ). If you change the trajectory's start, update these too, or the controller will slam a large one-shot correction the instant it activates. Troubleshooting ¶ Pendulum snaps hard the instant control starts. The URDF's initial_value params (in <ros2_control> ) don't match the trajectory generator's t=0 reference in control_node.py — keep them in sync. No motion / effort commands never arrive. Check that joint_state_broadcaster and effort_controller both spawned successfully ( ros2 control list_controllers ) — they're chained to start only after the model spawns, so a slow Gazebo startup can delay them, not fail them. Wrong torque direction / controller fights itself. This almost always means a joint axis or link-direction mismatch with the feedback-linearization model's convention — see the design note above before assuming it's a gain-tuning problem.

docs.text: 4.3 Exercise: Single Pendulum Swing-Up ¶ Build a single pendulum — one link, one revolute joint — in Gazebo, and drive it from hanging at rest up to the inverted (upright) equilibrium using the same feedback-linearization / computed-torque approach as dbpendulum_ctrl , just with one degree of freedom instead of two. The model ¶ A single pendulum's equation of motion is the one-link special case of dbpendulum 's dynamics — no coupling term between links, because there's only one link: M(theta) * thetaddot + C(theta, thetadot) + G(theta) = T with, for a single rigid link of mass m , moment of inertia I about its own center of mass, and pivot-to-COM distance c : M(theta) = I + m*c^2 # constant — no theta dependence for 1 DOF C(theta, thetadot) = 0 # no Coriolis/centrifugal term with only 1 joint G(theta) = m*g*c*sin(theta) # gravity torque, same functional form as dbpendulum's G1/G2 Two equilibria fall out of G(theta) = 0 : theta = 0 (hanging down, stable ) and theta = pi (inverted, unstable ) — same logic dbpendulum 's design notes walk through for the passive double pendulum's initial condition, just here you're driving the system to the unstable one on purpose, rather than starting near it. What to build ¶ Two packages, mirroring the dbpendulum / dbpendulum_ctrl split: single_pendulum — passive, visual-only sanity check first: single_pendulum/ ├── urdf/ │ └── single_pendulum.urdf.xacro ├── config/ │ └── single_pendulum_params.yaml # m, I, c, l ├── worlds/ │ └── single_pendulum_world.sdf ├── launch/ │ └── single_pendulum.launch.py └── config/ └── single_pendulum_bridge.yaml single_pendulum_ctrl — the actuated version: single_pendulum_ctrl/ ├── urdf/ │ └── single_pendulum.urdf.xacro # own copy — add <ros2_control> block ├── config/ │ ├── single_pendulum_ctrl_params.yaml # m, I, c, l, g, kp, kd │ └── controllers.yaml # joint_state_broadcaster + effort_controller ├── launch/ │ └── single_pendulum_ctrl.launch.py └── single_pendulum_ctrl/ ├── dynamics.py # M(theta), G(theta) closed-form ├── trajectory.py # theta_ref(t): 0 -> pi └── control_node.py # computed-torque law, publishes to effort_controller Suggested steps ¶ Passive version first. Get single_pendulum swinging freely under gravity before adding any control — same staged approach as dbpendulum . Confirm it hangs at theta = 0 at rest, and that a small push away from theta = 0 produces a normal pendulum swing. Design the reference trajectory. Pick a theta_ref(t) that goes smoothly from 0 to pi over some duration — a simple option is a single smooth point-to-point move (cubic or quintic polynomial in time), the single-joint analog of the two segments dbpendulum_ctrl uses for its two links. Implement the control law. Same structure as dbpendulum_ctrl 's controller, minus the coupling terms: T = M(theta) * (thetaddot_ref - Kp*(theta - theta_ref) - Kd*(thetadot - thetadot_ref)) + G(theta) Pick Kp / Kd critically damped, same convention as dbpendulum_ctrl : kd = 2*sqrt(kp) . Match gravity to Gazebo's default ( 9.8 , not 9.81 or 10 ) — dbpendulum_ctrl 's design notes explain why this has to match exactly for feedback linearization to actually cancel gravity. Wire up ros2_control . Same pattern as dbpendulum_ctrl : joint_state_broadcaster for state feedback, forward_command_controller/ForwardCommandController (interface effort ) as a pass-through for your computed torque — the actual control law lives in your node, not in a canned controller. Set the <ros2_control> initial_value to match your trajectory's theta(0) = 0 — if these don't match, expect the same "snaps hard the instant control starts" failure mode dbpendulum_ctrl 's troubleshooting section describes. Verify ¶ Log the tracking error ( theta - theta_ref ) over the run and confirm it stays small throughout, not just at the final instant — a controller that overshoots wildly and only happens to end near pi hasn't actually demonstrated tracking. Once it reaches theta = pi , it needs to stay there — since that equilibrium is unstable, this is really the point of the whole exercise: watch what happens if you cut the trajectory node before the tracking error has settled, versus after. Deliverables ¶ [ ] single_pendulum swinging passively under gravity [ ] single_pendulum_ctrl driving the joint from 0 to pi [ ] A plot or log showing tracking error settling near zero and staying there once theta_ref reaches pi [ ] A short note on what Kp / Kd you used and how you chose them
